pr_title: Allow alternate schemes in Kestrel requests
pr_body: Fixes #30532. Multiple HTTP/2 proxies for gRPC have been taking advantage of the `:scheme` header to forward the client's original scheme instead of using `x-forwarded-proto` headers. This change allows the developer to opt into mismatched schemes. Note the scheme must still be a valid format.

issue_context.title: GRPC :scheme pseudo-header passed from proxy/loadbalancer causes ConnectionAbortedException
issue_context.body:

For other types of questions, consider using [StackOverflow](https://stackoverflow.com).

### Describe the bug
Grpc kestrel .net 5 sample app greeter is running in k8s under http transport, an AWS network load balancer terminates SSL and sends request to the app with :scheme pseudo-header set to "https", but the actual transport is "http" results in this error -
`Trace id "0HM6QO8HEK1N9:00000001": HTTP/2 stream error "PROTOCOL_ERROR". A Reset is being sent to the stream.
Microsoft.AspNetCore.Connections.ConnectionAbortedException: The request :scheme header 'https' does not match the transport scheme 'http'.` 

The ask here is to be less stringent on validating on the :schema pseudo header, Go lang sample apps works fine.

### To Reproduce
<!--
We ❤ code! Point us to a minimalistic repro project hosted in a GitHub repo.
For a repro project, create a new ASP.NET Core project using the template of your your choice, apply the minimum required code to result in the issue you're observing.

We will close this issue if:
- the repro project you share with us is complex. We can't investigate custom projects, so don't point us to such, please.
- if we will not be able to repro the behavior you're reporting
-->
Deploy any sample grpc app from here - https://github.com/grpc/grpc-dotnet/tree/master/examples to k8s, setup the service type loadbalancer using AWS NLB. Test with grpcurl client.

### Exceptions (if any)
<!-- 
Include the exception you get when facing this issue
-->
`Microsoft.AspNetCore.Connections.ConnectionAbortedException: The request :scheme header 'https' does not match the transport scheme 'http'.`
### Further technical details
- ASP.NET Core version
- Include the output of `dotnet --info`
- The IDE (VS / VS Code/ VS4Mac) you're running on, and its version
comments:
Prior discussion: https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/14745. The main report was the result of a bug in the Java client. No concrete examples were given for the proxy scenario at the time.

The spec is extremely vague on the proper usage of this field so we opted for a strict interpretation until the scenarios could be clarified.

> an AWS network load balancer terminates SSL

Is this an L7 or L4 proxy? 
- For an L7 proxy it would make sense to run into this as it wouldn't understand the Http/2 protocol and wouldn't be able to make hop-by-hop modifications.
- For an L4 proxy the usage here is undefined. An L7 proxy would normally need to add x-forwarded-proto or Forwarded to headers to convey external information like the scheme.
Its a L4 proxy.
@blowdart What are your thoughts on making the `:scheme` header check less strict? Or adding an option to allow configuration?
Option, which you must opt into, with a suitable name like InsecureProtocolValidation. And scoped as narrowly as possible. So just to grpc.

The narrowest a setting like this could be scoped would be to an IP endpoint, and even that will be difficult. gRPC is a higher level protocol.

Scoping it to the whole server instance (KestrelServerOptions/Http2Limits) would be more consistent with our other HTTP/2 limits.

Thanks for contacting us.
We're moving this issue to the `Next sprint planning` milestone for future evaluation / consideration. We will evaluate the request when we are planning the work for the next milestone. To learn more about what to expect next and how this issue will be handled you can read more about our triage process [here](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/blob/master/docs/TriageProcess.md).

Is it possible to add an option to disable the server schema check? .NET is the only language that has this behavior. It'a arguably a correct implementation, but it causes a lot of user pains.

@MattyBoy4444 we'd have expected Envoy to send the https scheme as an x-forwarded-proto header and set the `:scheme` to http. Then ForwardedHeadersMiddleware would have been useful. As is, there's a hard block in the server that prevents it from accepting requests with `:scheme` values that don't match the transport. 

There's no workaround from the ASP.NET side other than using TLS between Envoy and Kestrel. I don't know if you can work around it from the Envoy end.
@davidfowl do we have kestrel ignore the scheme value, or do we have it honor it? E.g. should HttpRequest.Scheme show http or https? Envoy seems to intend this as a replacement for x-fowarded-proto.

>  Envoy seems to intend this as a replacement for x-fowarded-proto.

It would not be realistic to change all the cases to fit .NET enforcement, for example, if I use a managed proxy in front of .NET server, I just have no way to unblock myself. If .NET provides an config option, life would be much better.
We're discussing what the option does and we're going to get more data to see what competitors in the space do so we're well informed
Thanks. To add an additional data point: IIRC, all other languages with gRPC support don't (at least by default) have this enforcement on the h2c gRPC channel.
Which ones did you try? (you said *all*). Also do they change the scheme or do they ignore it?

Well, I have to say I  exaggerate :)

I tired the followings and they don't enforce the scheme for gRPC h2c channels: C++, Go, Java, Kotlin, Objective-C, Node, Python, Rust.

I don't know what happens underneath, for example, I am not sure if language itself doesn't check, or check bug ignore, or it provides an option which set by gRPC framework.

Envoy recently switched to using the original URL scheme or X-Forwarded-Proto as the request scheme recently:

"http: fixing a standards compliance issue with :scheme. The :scheme header sent upstream is now based on the original URL scheme, rather than set based on the security of the upstream connection. This behavior can be temporarily reverted by setting envoy.reloadable_features.preserve_downstream_scheme to false."

https://github.com/envoyproxy/envoy/issues/14587 is an interesting read, they seem to be re-thinking their stance on this.

This recently broke me in Cloud Run, I guess GCP updated envoy because it was working fine a couple of weeks ago.  Here's a workaround if anyone needs it:
1.  Download this repo, I use v5 so `git clone https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore.git && cd aspnetcore && git checkout tags/v5.0.5`
2. `git submodule update --init --recursive`
3. Find the file `/src/Servers/Kestrel/Core/src/Internal/Http2/Http2Stream.cs` and comment out lines 244-250.  If not version 5.0.5, it's the block of code that starts with `if (!ReferenceEquals(headerScheme, Scheme) &&`, comment that whole if block
4. build the project - `./build.sh --configuration Release` in the root of the project.  It had a few errors but the file I needed was built.
5. Take file `aspnetcore/artifacts/bin/Microsoft.AspNetCore.Server.Kestrel.Core/Release/net5.0/Microsoft.AspNetCore.Server.Kestrel.Core.dll` and copy it to a folder with the following Dockerfile:
```
FROM mcr.microsoft.com/dotnet/aspnet:5.0

COPY ./Microsoft.AspNetCore.Server.Kestrel.Core.dll /usr/share/dotnet/shared/Microsoft.AspNetCore.App/5.0.5/
```

Data point: IIS/Http.Sys also reject requests that have a mismatched scheme with the same RST_STREAM(PROTOCOL_ERROR). Note these servers only support HTTP/2 over TLS so the scheme must always be `https`.

The original poster indicated that the issue was with .NET 5, but I have confirm that it exists for .NET Core 3.1 also.  My hunch is that it's in the underlying gRPC framework implementation (but I'm sure you're aware of that).

I notice that @Tratcher 's [original comment](https://github.com/dotnet/aspnetcore/issues/30532#issuecomment-787011248) refers to the RFC spec being vague.  I agree.  I'm having a brief discussion with the Envoy team regarding their interpretation and can see both sides of the argument.

Since the Envoy team, and the [Istio team](https://github.com/istio/istio/issues/33136), are needing to deal with this issue (possibly specifically for .NET), I'm wondering if there is any indication from the .NET team about where their deliberations are heading (i.e. especially given that this issue has been marked with the `Next sprint planning` milestone)?  It would probably be helpful to those discussions to know whether this is something that needs to be dealt with in a long-term capacity.

Thanks.  :)

> My hunch is that it's in the underlying gRPC framework implementation (but I'm sure you're aware of that).

The restriction is in the HTTP servers themselves (Kestrel, Http.Sys, IIS).

> Since the Envoy team, and the [Istio team](https://github.com/istio/istio/issues/33136), are needing to deal with this issue (possibly specifically for .NET), I'm wondering if there is any indication from the .NET team about where their deliberations are heading (i.e. especially given that this issue has been marked with the `Next sprint planning` milestone)? It would probably be helpful to those discussions to know whether this is something that needs to be dealt with in a long-term capacity.

We do not expect the behavior to change in IIS or Http.Sys. We're considering a new .NET 6 API for Kestrel that would relax this restriction but haven't worked out the details yet.

The various providers and proxies have added configuration to mitigate this or have reverted the change. With the ambiguity in the spec this will likely need to be configurable in all proxies.

Thanks @Tratcher. I'm asking because the Envoy team is planning on retiring the flag that you reference in your link (see 
[Envoy 14587](https://github.com/envoyproxy/envoy/issues/14587#issuecomment-833663518)) and want to implement something less generic and more targeted for ongoing support.

Understanding the position of the .NET ecosystem (i.e. Kestrel may change but IIS and Http.Sys won't) is helpful and I'll respond accordingly.  Thanks.

We discussed putting this on the root Kestrel options at which point it would apply to HTTP/2 and HTTP/3. Most limits are currently numeric, so this seems like a slight outlier. On the other hand, it crowds the top-level option.

API feedback: Put this on the top level Kestrel option.

Additional discussion: Need to talk to @blowdart about enabling this option at all.

Updated API proposal:
```diff
public class KestrelServerOptions
{
+ /// <summary>
+ /// If disabled (default) then the `:scheme` field for HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 requests must exactly match the transport (e.g. https for TLS connections, http for non-TLS).
+ /// If enabled then the `:scheme` field for HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 requests can be set to alternate values and this will be reflected by `HttpRequest.Scheme`. Only enable this when working with a trusted proxy. This can be used in scenarios like proxies converting from alternate protocols. See https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc7540#section-8.1.2.3. Applications that enable this should validate an expected scheme is provided before using it for link generation, etc. 
+ /// </summary>
+ public bool AllowAlternateSchemes { get; set; } = false;
}
```
I grudgingly approve, with the proviso there's a warning about the security in the xml docs. Maybe an aka.ms links to a doc explaining the issue in detail as well?

review_comments: The validation only happens if you allow alternate schemes. Verbosely it would be AllowAndValidateAlternateSchemes.
The API was approved, its fine I guess.
CheckSchemeName is a new check, perf?

Note this new check only happens after the standard match checks have failed and you've opted into AllowAlternateSchemes, there should be no impact on the normal scenario.
